title: Which duplicate-payment defense holds
question: **Campaign running; results pending: this page shows requirements, design, predictions and controls only.** A payment service records each payment in its own database and publishes it to Kafka; a ledger consumer applies it to balances in a second Postgres. Under real broker, process and network faults, which defense keeps every recorded payment applied exactly once: none (N), [Kafka transactions](p3:idempotence) (K), an [idempotency key at the sink](p3:key) (I), or an [outbox](p3:dualwrite) plus that key (O+I)? And at which boundary does each one stop? One laptop, public software, 760 pre-registered trials.

requirements.text: Every payment committed in the source database is applied exactly once, and every balance equals opening + credits − debits over the source's payments, computed without reading anything the consumer wrote.
requirements.why: The source row is the business record of the payment. Conservation alone is useless here: double-entry keeps the total constant, so a duplicate or a loss never trips it. The review upgraded the invariant to per-account reconciliation.

requirements.short: Say where each anomaly was born
requirements.text: Attribute every loss and every extra apply to the producer side (source ↔ Kafka), the consumer side (Kafka ↔ ledger), or unattributable.
requirements.why: The defenses guard different boundaries, so a count without a birthplace cannot say which one failed. Unattributable applies are reported, never split by guesswork.

requirements.text: Compare whole pipelines in which each contrast, N→K, N→I and I→O+I, adds exactly one defense.
requirements.why: The four defenses do not sit on one axis: ranked head to head, they would compare things at different layers.

requirements.short: Real faults: whether, and how often
requirements.text: Inject real kills, pauses and network blackholes, at code hooks in the weakest window (can it break?) and at random times (how often?), and confirm each fault took effect.
requirements.why: The closest prior work simulated its faults inside the application. Random faults rarely land in narrow windows, so without targeted cells a zero would mean little.

requirements.short: A zero must be able to fail
requirements.text: Before the campaign, show in real trials that the checker catches a duplicate and a loss when they happen, and stays silent when no fault runs.
requirements.why: A zero only means something if the harness can see a nonzero ([controls](p3:controls)).

requirements.text: Commit the hypotheses, fault matrix, void rules, gate and analysis before the first measured trial; no early stopping, no extension, and no anomaly output read until the campaign ends.
requirements.why: With 4 stacks × 9 cells, a result can be argued into shape afterwards. A [pre-registration](p2:prereg) tag and dated [amendments](p2:amendment) show which rules came first; reconnaissance ran before the tag and is not a result.

concepts.plain: Same client, topic, two consumers, schema and failure policy; only the defense differs. **N**: dual write, [at-least-once](p3:atleast) consumer. **K**: dual write, consumer offsets inside a Kafka transaction. **I**: dual write, key checked in the ledger transaction. **O+I**: outbox relayed by Debezium, plus the key. **N→K**, **N→I** and **I→O+I** each add one defense. Every producer is idempotent; O+I's needs a config override.

Six faults plus a no-fault control (F0); the design matrix names them and the boundary map shows which gap each tests. F5 is a [zombie](p3:groups) consumer. **Random-time** cells (F1–F3, F4-con-r; 30 trials per stack, as for F0) ask how often; **targeted** cells (a code hook; 10 trials) ask whether.

The share of a consumer's running time between its ledger `COMMIT` returning and its Kafka progress committing (`commitSync` for N and I, `commitTransaction` for K), measured in F0 trials over 20–50 s, the window random kills draw from (the analysis sums both consumers' windows over 60 s). A random kill duplicates only if it lands inside the window, so the duty cycle should predict the F4-con-r duplicate rate (H5).

A **block** is one cell and one seed run on all four stacks in random order: the same fault schedule and payment stream. A void trial voids its whole block, re-run with a new seed, so analysed blocks stay [paired](p2:pairing). For N vs K, the exact McNemar test uses only blocks where exactly one of the two had a duplicate (**discordant**); Newcombe's paired interval (method 10), over all the cell's blocks, gives a plausible range for the difference. Two contrasts are confirmatory: N vs K in F4-con-r (H5) and in F1+F2 (H4b).

concepts.short: What zero in N trials claims
concepts.plain: The trial is the unit: payments in one trial share a fault and are never pooled. If 0 of N trials show an anomaly, the per-trial probability is below 1 − 0.05^(1/N), one-sided 95%. The **rule of three**, about 3/N, approximates it.

Run after the pre-registration tag, before the campaign, and not counted in it: the checker on synthetic histories, two [positive controls](p3:controls) on **N only**, and a negative control of five no-fault trials per stack. All four must pass; the rules are in the gate chart below.

walkthrough.title: One K batch, killed in the commit window
walkthrough.lead: A prediction (H1), not a result: values illustrate one payment, from the code and pre-registration. Only N has been seen duplicating this way (in the gate); K's abort-and-recommit path has not been run.

steps.say: K polls a batch. `beginTransaction()` is client-local: the broker has heard nothing, so a kill now would leave no Kafka transaction to abort.
The ledger transaction commits to Postgres first. Kafka is not part of it, so this row is permanent whatever Kafka does next.

K sends the record and adds its offsets: open, nothing visible. In one recon run (pre-campaign), 67% and 65% of transactions retried the offset commit after ~100 ms, widening [this window](a6:window) (H5).
F4-con-t sends SIGKILL at `before_kafka_commit`: row committed, transaction open and never finished. Nothing in the dead process can undo the row.
It restarts 5 s later; `initTransactions()` on the same `transactional.id` aborts the open transaction. Had it not come back, `transaction.timeout.ms` (60 s default) would.
The offsets were never committed, so the group resumes from the last committed offset and delivers the same batch again.
K has no key check, so the Postgres commit runs again, and K sends the record in a new Kafka transaction. The ledger has the batch twice; Postgres was never in the aborted one.

If nothing interferes, the second `commitTransaction` succeeds: offsets move on. A `read_committed` reader sees the payment once, a `read_uncommitted` one also the aborted copy. Kafka is consistent; the ledger is not.

walkthrough.takeaway: Output once, ledger twice: Kafka's transaction ended cleanly, but Postgres was never in it. H1 needs ledger duplicates in at least 8 of 10 F4-con-t trials (output once is reported beside it). No K result here.

walkthrough.title: A producer-side loss: killed after the source commit
walkthrough.lead: Observed in the detection gate on stack N (`gate_prod_1`, cell F4-svc), not a campaign result. H3 predicts K and I lose too.

steps.say: The client sends `p00004003`; the service commits it to the source database. The payment now exists, and the source is the authority.
The `after_source_commit` hook holds the service: committed, nothing sent. The orchestrator sees the fire 61 ms later and kills the service 424 ms after it fired.
The send never happens. Two payments reached the source in the 240 ms around the hook and were never published: this one and one other in-flight request.
The client saw both as `info` (timeout or reset), never `ok`. The service restarts after 5 s.
The checker finds the payment in the source and not in the topic: a loss with a topic gap, born on the producer side.

walkthrough.takeaway: Gap P: a crash between source commit and send loses the payment. H3 predicts O+I, whose outbox row is written in the source commit, loses none.

walkthrough.title: A zombie consumer: paused, replaced, then it writes
walkthrough.lead: Observed on N in reconnaissance (all 17 F5 trials), except step 3. K and I are predictions (H1, H2).

steps.say: A polls a batch; the `after_poll` hook holds it and the orchestrator runs `docker pause` on A. Batch in hand, no database work yet.
With no heartbeat for `session.timeout.ms` (10 s), the coordinator moves A's partitions to B. In all 17 recon trials the generation went from 1 to 2 while A was paused.
B resumes from the last committed offset, gets the same batch and applies it (documented semantics; not in the recon record).

A unpauses 5 to 20 s (seeded) past the session timeout. Its first act is the `db_commit` of its held batch; Postgres cannot tell A is stale. About 0.1 s on, its offset commit is refused with `CommitFailedException`.
Crash-only: A exits and restarts into the next generation. Fencing stopped the Kafka commit, not the ledger write.

walkthrough.takeaway: The zombie wrote, then its commit failed; the ledger holds the payment twice if B applied first. H1 predicts the same for K; H2, that I's key insert skips.

decisions.title: Whole pipelines, one change each
decisions.problem: The brief listed four defenses as alternatives, but the outbox guards the producer side, Kafka transactions cover only Kafka-to-Kafka work, and the key works at the sink.
options: Rank the four defenses head to head
Add offsets stored in Postgres as a fifth arm
Leave Connect's default, the relay producer's idempotence off
Four whole pipelines, N, K, I and O+I, each contrast adding one defense, every producer idempotent
decisions.chosen: Four whole pipelines, N, K, I and O+I, each contrast adding one defense, every producer idempotent
decisions.why: Ranked head to head the defenses would compare things at different layers. Offsets in Postgres is correct and Kafka's docs recommend it, but it guards the consumer side as I does and breaks the three-contrast structure. With Connect's default, I→O+I would change two things at once. The client assigns `payment_id` at the origin, and every defense depends on that.
decisions.cost: A reader running Debezium as shipped has a non-idempotent relay (`max.in.flight=1`) whose retries can duplicate: stated, not measured. Offsets in Postgres and KIP-618's exactly-once source are explained or named, not measured.
decisions.why_short: Ranked head to head the defenses would compare different layers; whole pipelines let each contrast add exactly one.
decisions.cost_short: Debezium's shipped default (a non-idempotent relay) and offsets in Postgres are explained, not measured.

serves.because: N→K, N→I and I→O+I each add one defense; forcing the relay idempotent keeps I→O+I to one change.
Each defense sits at the boundary it guards, so an anomaly's birthplace names the defense that missed it.

decisions.title: Postgres first, one state at the hook
decisions.problem: A crash between the ledger commit and Kafka's progress commit is where consumer-side duplicates are born, so the order of the two commits, and where the targeted kill lands, decide what is measured.
options: Commit Kafka first, then Postgres
Kill K before any Kafka work (the first draft's hook)
Postgres first in every mode; `before_kafka_commit` placed per mode, for K after `sendOffsetsToTransaction`
decisions.chosen: Postgres first in every mode; `before_kafka_commit` placed per mode, for K after `sendOffsetsToTransaction`
decisions.why: Postgres first is the common order; the reverse trades duplicates for losses, which the post states by reasoning and does not measure. At the first draft's hook K had no broker-side transaction, so K and N ran the same code path; the review moved it. Now every stack is hit with the ledger committed and Kafka's progress not.
decisions.cost: Results hold for this commit order only: a reader whose Postgres commits after Kafka is outside what is measured. K's commit step also carries Kafka's default ~100 ms `CONCURRENT_TRANSACTIONS` retry (reconnaissance; rates in How it works); it is left as is, named, and lengthens the window H5 measures.
decisions.why_short: The common order, and one state for every stack at the hook: ledger committed, Kafka progress not; for K, a real open transaction.
decisions.cost_short: Kafka-first consumers are outside what is measured; K keeps Kafka's default ~100 ms commit retry.
decisions.short: Postgres first, one state at the hook

serves.because: The targeted cell F4-con-t can only ask whether a stack breaks if the kill lands in the same window for each.
The same commit order in every mode keeps N→K about the transaction, not about ordering.

uses.because: The hook sits inside the commit window; H5 measures how much time each stack spends there.
F4-con-t is the cell that fires this hook.

decisions.title: Crash-only, every mode
decisions.problem: Outcomes in F1, F2, F5 and F6 depend on what a consumer does on an error; error handling must not become a second variable between stacks.
options: Textbook in-process recovery: abort, seek, continue
Crash-only: any exception in apply or commit rolls back if it can, logs, and halts; a supervisor restarts the process after 2 s
decisions.chosen: Crash-only: any exception in apply or commit rolls back if it can, logs, and halts; a supervisor restarts the process after 2 s
decisions.why: For these exceptions crash-only reaches the textbook outcome, resuming from the last committed offsets, and it is what an orchestrated deployment does by default. It removes the abort, seek and continue path, where a missed `seek` silently skips a batch and where KAFKA-17582 would act. The exit is `Runtime.halt(1)` with no client closed, so every crash looks the same to the group and the coordinator.
decisions.cost: In-process recovery is unmeasured and named out of scope. A loss hypothesis about KAFKA-17582 was dropped before pre-registration: this design gives the bug no route to the ledger, so a zero would have read as evidence it never had.
decisions.why_short: It reaches the textbook outcome, is what orchestrators do by default, and removes the skip-prone in-process path.
decisions.cost_short: In-process recovery is unmeasured; the KAFKA-17582 loss hypothesis was dropped, not tested.

serves.because: One policy for N, K and I keeps error handling out of every contrast.

uses.because: The policy is shared by every stack, like the client and schema.

decisions.title: Real faults, checked
decisions.problem: A defense can only be judged against faults that really happen to processes and the network, and a fault that silently did nothing would produce a false zero.
options: Simulate faults inside the application, as the closest prior work does
One Toxiproxy in front of the bootstrap address
Random-time faults only
Real kills, pauses and blackholes via per-role proxies; random (30) and targeted (10) cells; a check per cell
decisions.chosen: Real kills, pauses and blackholes via per-role proxies; random (30) and targeted (10) cells; a check per cell
decisions.why: Simulated faults are what the closest prior work used. Clients connect to what brokers advertise, so one bootstrap proxy would fault nothing after the first metadata response. Targeted cells ask whether, random cells how often. The [manipulation check](p3:injector) reads only orchestrator, broker and process state; a failed check voids the trial and its block, and no trial is voided for what the checker found.
decisions.cost: One laptop: combined KRaft, no database failover, no disk faults, no inter-broker partitions. Host contention needed two added void reasons (`host_swap_out`, then `host_degraded` in amendment A1); contention that starts after 20 s is not caught.
decisions.why_short: Simulated faults are what the closest prior work did; targeted cells ask whether, random cells how often, and each fault is checked.
decisions.cost_short: One laptop and its limits; host contention needed two extra void reasons, and late contention is not caught.

serves.because: Nine cells with two timings, each fault confirmed by a check that never reads the ledger.
A fault that did nothing voids its block instead of passing as a clean zero.

uses.because: The matrix is this decision in table form.

decisions.title: Source as oracle, apply log
decisions.problem: To say 'applied exactly once' and 'born here', the checker needs a truth independent of the consumer and a record of each apply's `(partition, offset)`.
options: A unique applied table
An 'unknown' bucket for timed-out requests
A linearizability checker
Count each payment in the source, topic and append-only `apply_log`; the source resolves `info`; attribute by offset
decisions.chosen: Count each payment in the source, topic and append-only `apply_log`; the source resolves `info`; attribute by offset
decisions.why: A unique applied table would hide the very duplicates N and K are expected to produce. The review dropped 'unknown' because it contradicted the source-as-authority rule. With unique IDs and commuting increments, [counting each ID](p3:history) is a complete check, and order is not part of the invariant, so no linearizability checker is needed. The offset splits a duplicate into a redelivery or a re-send.
decisions.cost: Order is not checked: a defense that holds here may not hold for a ledger with overdraft rules. The experiment can resolve `info`; a real client cannot. An apply whose offset is absent from the readback stays unattributable.
decisions.why_short: A unique table would hide the duplicates; the source as oracle and each apply's offset make the check complete and attributable.
decisions.cost_short: No ordering check, so overdraft-style ledgers are out; `info` is resolvable only because this is an experiment.

serves.because: Expected balances come from the source alone, never from what the consumer wrote.
Same offset: consumer side; different offset: producer side; offset missing: unattributable.

uses.because: The gate tested this checker on synthetic histories and on real controls.

decisions.title: Pre-register, gate, pair, seal
decisions.problem: With 4 stacks × 9 cells on a noisy laptop, a result could be argued into shape afterwards, and a blind checker would give false zeros.
options: Pool payments into a per-payment rate
Look at results mid-campaign; stop early or extend
Newcombe's method 8, as the plan's code first had it
Against host contention: an operating condition, or a mechanical guard
Rules tagged first; a detection gate; paired blocks with method 10 and McNemar; both contention fixes; a sealed campaign
decisions.chosen: Rules tagged first; a detection gate; paired blocks with method 10 and McNemar; both contention fixes; a sealed campaign
decisions.why: Payments in one trial share a fault, so the trial is the unit. Not reading results rules out any decision that depends on them. The implementer found the plan's φ lacked method 10's continuity correction (that is method 8); plan and code were fixed and checked against Newcombe's Table III before the campaign-v1 tag. The gate showed contention degrading 5 of 42 trials, so amendment A1 chose both the condition and a guard.
decisions.cost: About 50–55 h of unattended runtime, and 30 trials per stack resolve only large differences, so H5 may end inconclusive. Reconnaissance ran before the tag; one rule (C-R, on cap refusals) was set after seeing its data, disclosed. The gate's positive controls ran on N only.
decisions.why_short: Timestamped rules, a gate that can see a nonzero, paired blocks and an unread campaign keep the rules ahead of the data.
decisions.cost_short: 50–55 h of runtime; H5 may be inconclusive; positive controls on N only; one recon rule set after its data.

serves.because: The gate's controls run before the campaign and must pass before it may start.
prereg-v1 precedes every gate and campaign trial; campaign-v1 precedes the first campaign trial.

uses.because: Paired blocks make N vs K a paired contrast with McNemar and Newcombe.
A clean cell is reported as a bound, not as safety.
The gate is the control that makes a zero meaningful.

flow.label: Reframe the brief into a two-boundary experiment
flow.detail: First draft; an independent review moved K's hook, added the crash-only policy, H5, the producer and negative controls and per-account reconciliation; approved the same day.
flow.output: the approved spec: 4 stacks, 9 cells, H1–H6 with falsifiers, the detection gate, a learning guide

flow.label: Cluster, per-role listeners, service and consumers
flow.detail: Three combined KRaft nodes; nine role proxies, verified by blackholing one role (F3 kept); the service in dual-write and outbox modes; consumers N and I, then K with Postgres first, all crash-only.
flow.output: a runnable pipeline in every stack mode; no fault injection yet

flow.label: Checker on synthetic histories
flow.detail: Counting over source, topic readback and apply_log; every anomaly class and attribution row tested on synthetic fixtures.
flow.output: checker/: classification and attribution per spec §6

flow.label: Reconnaissance A: rate, VM, K's commit step
flow.detail: The rate rule failed first; after seeing that data it stopped counting cap refusals as errors (C-R, disclosed). VM stalls traced to the host swapping the Docker VM. `diag_k1` explained K's flat ~148 ms commit step. Values frozen, then re-verified on an 8 GB VM.
flow.output: docs/recon-part-a.md: 200/s, 8 GB VM, 512m heaps, swappiness 1; "Nothing here is a result."

flow.output: orchestrator/ and manip/: every cell injectable, every trial gets a verdict

flow.label: Reconnaissance B: F2, F5, F6 and the checks
flow.detail: F2's first set stopped on an observer bug, a harness error, fixed; F5's count restarted after host-swap voids (the zombie is traced in How it works). F6 kept at 10 of 10.
flow.output: docs/recon-part-b.md: session.timeout.ms 10 s, F2 20–60 s, F6 kept; part B frozen

flow.label: Pre-register, tag prereg-v1
flow.detail: docs/experiment.md copies the spec's hypotheses, matrix, checks, gate and analysis verbatim by line range, with reconnaissance's frozen values and dated amendments. Tagged after reconnaissance, before any gate or campaign trial.

flow.label: Run the detection gate
flow.detail: The evaluator was committed minutes after the tag, before the first gate trial. 42 trials, two voids replaced. Five showed host contention; that became amendment A1.
flow.output: docs/gate.md: GATE PASS; positive controls on N only

flow.label: Contention guard, block plan and runner
flow.detail: `host_degraded` voids a campaign trial with over 100 cap refusals in its 5–20 s window; the 190-block plan is derived by code and committed; the runner resumes, replaces void blocks and reads only harness integrity.

flow.label: Analysis code, with the Newcombe method fix
flow.detail: Writing the statistics, the implementer noted the plan's φ had no continuity correction: Newcombe's method 8, not the pre-registered method 10. Plan and code were fixed within a minute and checked on Table III: 18, 12, 2, 18 gives 0.0562 to 0.3290.
flow.output: analysis/: Wilson, zero bound, Newcombe method 10, exact McNemar, H1–H6 evaluators

interview.pitch30: I built a fault-injection harness that asks which duplicate-payment defense holds between Kafka and a Postgres ledger: none, Kafka transactions, an idempotency key at the sink, or an outbox plus that key. Real kills, pauses and blackholes hit each pipeline, and a checker with the source database as the authority says whether every payment was applied exactly once and where any anomaly was born. A detection gate on the naive stack caught a duplicate and a loss, 10 of 10 each. The predictions were tagged before any gate or campaign trial; the campaign's results are sealed until it ends.
interview.pitch120: Teams say "exactly-once", but the usual defenses guard different boundaries: the outbox the producer side, Kafka transactions only Kafka-to-Kafka work, an idempotency key the sink. So I built four whole pipelines, each contrast adding one defense, on one laptop with public software, and a harness that injects real faults: broker kills and pauses, a producer blackhole, consumer kills at random times and at a code hook in the commit window, a zombie consumer, a lost COMMIT reply. A checker treats the source database as the authority and uses each apply's (partition, offset) to tell a redelivery from a re-send. The rules were tagged after reconnaissance and before the first gate trial, with dated amendments before the first campaign trial. H1 predicts Kafka transactions still double-post when killed after the Postgres commit. H5, the non-obvious one, predicts they make a random crash more likely to double-post, because the transaction commit widens the window between the ledger commit and Kafka's progress. A detection gate on the naive stack showed the checker sees a duplicate and a loss when they happen. The 760-trial campaign is running and I don't read its anomaly output until it ends, so today I can give you the design and the bets, not the answers.

followups.q: Do your consumers commit the database before or after Kafka, and what does that do to your duplicate rate under crashes?
followups.a: Postgres first, then Kafka's progress, in every stack. A crash between the two leaves the ledger committed and the offset not, so the batch is redelivered and applied again unless the sink checks a key; the gate showed it on N, the record at (1, 646) applied again 10.1 s later. Kafka first trades duplicates for losses; that I state by reasoning, not measurement. How often a random crash lands in the window depends on the time spent there: H5 predicts K spends more, because of the ~100 ms commit retry reconnaissance saw (How it works, step 3). The campaign will measure the rates.

followups.q: Kafka has exactly-once. Why doesn't K solve it?
followups.a: A Kafka transaction commits Kafka partitions and consumer offsets atomically; Postgres is not a participant, and KIP-939, two-phase commit with external participants, had not shipped as of October 2026 (its code was reverted for Kafka 4.2). By the documented semantics, a kill after K's Postgres commit and before `commitTransaction` ends in an abort, a redelivery and a second Postgres commit (How it works). H1 predicts duplicates in at least 8 of 10 such trials, and in the zombie cell; the campaign will say.

followups.q: Why not store offsets in Postgres in the same transaction?
followups.a: It is correct, Kafka's docs recommend it, and it guards the consumer side as I does; as a fifth arm it would break the one-change contrasts. It deduplicates by (partition, offset), though, and an outbox relay's re-send lands at a new offset, so it would not catch O+I's relay duplicates. Only a key carried from the origin catches those.

followups.q: How do you know a zero isn't a blind checker, or a fault that never happened?
followups.a: The detection gate, run after the tag: 44 synthetic tests covering 26 class and attribution rows; on N, commit-window kills gave a consumer-side duplicate in 10 of 10 trials and kills after the source commit a producer-side loss in 10 of 10; 20 of 20 no-fault trials across the four stacks were clean. Every campaign trial also gets a per-cell manipulation check that never reads the ledger; a failed one voids the block. The gap: the positive controls ran on N only.

followups.q: Your zombie consumer: which fencing stops it, and does it stop the duplicate write?
followups.a: Generation fencing, at the offset commit: the group coordinator rejects a commit from an old generation. On N that is the ordinary check on `commitSync` in the classic group protocol; KIP-447 added the same check to K's `TxnOffsetCommit`. In reconnaissance on N, in all 17 F5 trials, the paused consumer's first act after unpause was a `db_commit` of the batch it held, then `CommitFailedException` about 0.1 s later. The Postgres write is another system's commit and has already happened, so fencing stops the Kafka commit, not the ledger write. Epoch fencing protects a `transactional.id` from its own earlier incarnation, and it is what aborts K's open transaction when K restarts. It cannot stop this zombie, because the consumer that took the partitions has its own `transactional.id`. For K, H1 predicts the same duplicate at `TxnOffsetCommit`.

followups.q: What came before your pre-registration tag?
followups.a: Reconnaissance A and B: the rate, the VM, Debezium's lifecycle, the F2, F5 and F6 decision rules, and the manipulation checks on real trials. Their values were frozen into the pre-registration and none is reported as a result. One recon rule (C-R: cap refusals are not rate-rule errors) was set after seeing data, and is disclosed. The tag came before any gate or campaign trial, and the analysis code and amendments A1–A4 were tagged campaign-v1 before the first campaign trial.

interview.limits: No campaign result is reported here: the campaign is running and its anomaly output is unread, so nothing here says which defense held. The gate's positive controls ran on N only; nothing yet shows K duplicating. When results exist they will hold for one laptop (combined KRaft, one Docker VM), this configuration (acks=all, Postgres before Kafka, crash-only recovery, the classic group protocol, these versions) and these faults; no overdraft rule, so ordering is untested; no database failover, disk faults or inter-broker partitions; client retries to the API are excluded; no production fault frequency is claimed. Reconnaissance numbers come from earlier environments and are not results.

recall.q: Under F4-svc, how does a dual-write stack lose a payment, and why should O+I not?
recall.a: The service commits the source row, is killed before sending, and the payment never reaches the topic: a loss with a topic gap, born on the producer side. O+I writes the outbox row in the same commit, and the relay publishes it later.

recall.q: Where does the commit-window hook sit for K, and why not before the Kafka work?
recall.a: After the Postgres commit, the payments-applied sends and `sendOffsetsToTransaction`, before `commitTransaction`. Earlier the broker has no transaction yet (How it works, step 1), so K would run N's code path.

recall.q: In `gate_cons_1`, what tells the checker the duplicate was born on the consumer side?
recall.a: The extra apply has the same (partition, offset), (1, 646), as the first: a redelivery. A different offset for the same payment would mean a re-send, born on the producer side.

recall.q: Why pair random-time cells with targeted cells?
recall.a: Random faults rarely land in narrow windows, so a random zero alone would mean little. Targeted cells ask whether a defense can break at all; random cells how often it does under realistic timing.

recall.q: Suppose I shows 0 anomalies in 30 trials of a cell. What could you claim?
recall.a: That its per-trial probability for that fault is below about 9.5% (one-sided 95%), on this setup. Not that the defense is safe in general.

recall.q: Why does one void trial void its whole block?
recall.a: So every analysed block keeps all four stacks with the same fault schedule and payment stream: the pairing the N vs K contrasts rely on. The block is re-run with a new seed.

recall.q: What is the commit-window duty cycle, and why should it predict F4-con-r duplicates?
recall.a: The share of running time between a ledger `COMMIT` returning and Kafka progress committing. A random kill duplicates only if it lands in that window, so a wider window should mean more duplicates (H5).

recall.q: Why is a trial voided by a failed manipulation check but never by the checker's output?
recall.a: The check asks whether the fault happened, from orchestrator, broker and process state. Voiding on the checker's output would let results decide which trials count.

recall.q: Why crash-only rather than in-process recovery?
recall.a: It reaches the same outcome (resume from the last committed offsets), is what orchestrators do by default, keeps error handling out of the contrasts, and removes the abort-seek-continue path where skip bugs live.

recall.q: What does the passed detection gate not tell you?
recall.a: Anything about K, I or O+I under faults: both positive controls ran on N. Nor any campaign rate: the gate's trials are not counted in the campaign.
